lessons.title: Deep brain stimulation: several mechanisms, one electrode, and the difference between a pre-post change and a treatment effect
lessons.explanation:
Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to describe the physical parameters of deep brain stimulation, state the competing mechanistic accounts, explain why the microlesion effect and unblinding matter, and interpret an open-label series against a sham-controlled trial. Lesson 69 established what different trial designs can show; lesson 88 established the logic of reversible perturbation at the cortical surface. This lesson applies both to stimulation delivered through an electrode implanted in the basal ganglia or thalamus, where the parameters are known exactly and the mechanism is still disputed.

The device is a pacemaker-like generator connected to a quadripolar electrode implanted stereotactically. Each contact is a cylinder of about one millimetre in diameter and one to two millimetres in length, and the contacts are separated by a fraction of a millimetre to a few millimetres. Stimulation is usually continuous and monopolar, with a typical frequency of about 130 to 185 Hz, a pulse width of 60 to 90 microseconds, and an amplitude of one to five volts or two to four milliamperes, adjusted to the patient. The targets are anatomically specific: the subthalamic nucleus and the globus pallidus internus for Parkinson disease, the ventral intermediate nucleus of the thalamus for tremor, the globus pallidus internus for dystonia, and the anterior nucleus of the thalamus for some forms of epilepsy. Each target has a different evidence base, and a result in one cannot be transferred to another.

The mechanism is the most contested part, and the contest is instructive. At the intensity used clinically, the electric field is largest within a few millimetres of the contact and falls steeply. Three families of explanation are current. The first is local modulation: high-frequency stimulation suppresses somatic firing near the electrode, either through depolarisation block or through activation of inhibitory terminals, while simultaneously activating axons passing through the region, including the corticosubthalamic and pallidothalamic pathways. The second is network modulation: the stimulation disrupts pathological oscillatory activity, particularly the beta band activity at 13 to 30 Hz that is elevated in the subthalamic nucleus in Parkinson disease and that falls when dopamine replacement is given. The third is synaptic and metabolic: stimulation changes neurotransmitter release, including glutamate and adenosine, and may produce effects that outlast the stimulus.

Herrington, Chaturvedi and colleagues (Journal of Neurophysiology, 2016) review these accounts and make the point that they are not exclusive: local and network-wide electrical and neurochemical effects, modulation of oscillatory activity, synaptic plasticity and possibly neuroprotective effects all vary in importance depending on the condition and the target. That is an unusually honest position for a review, and it has a methodological consequence: a study that measures one mechanism and finds it present has not excluded the others, and a study that finds it absent has not excluded the therapy.

The clinical evidence has a characteristic structure. Open-label series report large improvements from baseline: 40 to 50 per cent reductions in motor scores are common in Parkinson disease, and patients and clinicians can see the change when the device is switched on. Randomised trials with sham stimulation report smaller differences between active and sham arms, typically in the range of 10 to 20 percentage points on the same scales. The gap between the two is not a scandal; it is the expected consequence of regression to the mean, expectation, attention, the microlesion effect of electrode insertion and the difficulty of blinding.

The microlesion effect deserves emphasis because it is measurable and often large. Insertion of the electrode produces local oedema and a small lesion, and many patients improve before the device is switched on. A trial that compares stimulation on against stimulation off, with the electrode already in place, controls for that effect; a trial that compares surgery plus stimulation against baseline does not. Blinding is the second issue: stimulation can produce paraesthesias, muscle contractions, dysarthria and changes in handwriting, so patients and assessors can often tell whether the device is active. The best trials assess the success of blinding and report it.

The correct unit of analysis follows from these considerations. The treatment effect is the difference between active and control conditions in a randomised comparison, not the change from baseline. The pre-post change answers a different question, namely how much patients improved under a package of surgery, programming and care, and it is a legitimate clinical quantity. Confusing the two produces the pattern in which a device appears to be twice as effective in an open-label series as in a trial.
lessons.example:
Work the electrical and the clinical arithmetic, then separate the quantities.

Step 1, the pulse. At 130 Hz the interval between pulses is 1000 divided by 130, or about 7.7 milliseconds. A pulse of 90 microseconds occupies 90 divided by 7692 of that interval, or about 1.2 per cent of the time. The tissue is therefore stimulated for roughly 12 milliseconds in every second and unstimulated for the rest, which is why the effect cannot be a simple continuous inhibition of the target.

Step 2, the charge. For a 3 volt pulse delivered through an impedance of about 1000 ohms, the peak current is about 3 milliamperes and the charge per pulse is 3 milliamperes times 90 microseconds, or about 0.27 microcoulombs. The energy per pulse is the voltage times the charge, about 0.81 microjoules, and at 130 pulses per second that is about 105 microwatts.

Step 3, the battery. A typical implantable generator stores on the order of 13 kilojoules. Dividing 13,000 joules by 105 microwatts gives about 124 million seconds, or roughly four years of continuous stimulation at these settings, which is the right order of magnitude for the replacement interval reported in practice. The arithmetic is worth doing because it shows how little energy the brain receives and how much of the clinical effect must come from modulating an existing circuit rather than from driving it.

Step 4, the open-label number. A series reports a 45 per cent improvement in motor scores at six months compared with baseline. That number includes the surgery, the programming, the attention of a specialist team, the microlesion effect and the natural fluctuation of the disease. It is a real description of what happened to those patients and it is not an estimate of the effect of the electrical stimulation.

Step 5, the trial number. A randomised trial reports 22 per cent improvement on active stimulation and 12 per cent on sham. The stimulation-specific effect is the difference between arms, 10 percentage points, and the number needed to treat for one additional patient to reach a response criterion, if response rates were 55 per cent and 35 per cent, would be 100 divided by 20, or 5.

Step 6, the reconciliation. Both numbers are correct, and they answer different questions. The open-label change is the effect of a treatment package; the randomised difference is the effect of the current. Reporting only the first overstates the device, and reporting only the second discards information about the total benefit that patients experience.
lessons.question: An open-label trial of deep brain stimulation for treatment-resistant depression reports a 50 per cent response rate at twelve months, while a later randomised trial with sham stimulation finds no difference between active and sham arms. Which explanation is most consistent with the evidence?
lessons.answer: Open-label response combines stimulation with expectation, attention, the microlesion effect and regression to the mean, while the sham-controlled comparison removes those components, so a large unblinded response with a null controlled effect is the signature of a non-specific response rather than a contradiction.
lessons.distractor: The randomised trial must have used incorrect stimulation parameters, since a well-placed electrode with adequate current could not fail to produce the open-label effect.
lessons.correction: The parameter explanation is possible in principle and is not supported by the pattern: when a therapy shows a large open-label effect and no controlled effect across multiple targets and teams, the more economical explanation is that the open-label effect is largely non-specific. Depression trials are especially vulnerable because response is measured by rating scales that are sensitive to attention and hope, participants are often severely ill and motivated, and the surgery itself is a powerful event. The correct conclusion is not that stimulation has no biological effect; it is that the biological effect has not been shown to exceed the non-specific effect in a controlled comparison. A parameter optimisation hypothesis would need a controlled trial that varies parameters and still shows an advantage over sham.

depth.definitions: Deep brain stimulation is the delivery of continuous electrical pulses through an implanted electrode to a subcortical target. A quadripolar electrode has four cylindrical contacts, and the contact configuration determines the shape of the electric field. The pulse width is the duration of each pulse, the frequency is the number of pulses per second, and the amplitude is the voltage or current delivered. Monopolar stimulation uses one contact as the cathode and the generator case as the anode, producing a wider field than bipolar stimulation between two contacts. The microlesion effect is the improvement produced by electrode insertion itself, before stimulation begins. Beta band activity is oscillatory activity at 13 to 30 Hz, elevated in the subthalamic nucleus in Parkinson disease. Adaptive or closed-loop stimulation adjusts the amplitude in response to a measured biomarker such as beta power. Sham stimulation in surgical trials means the device is implanted but not activated, or activated at a subthreshold setting. Prerequisites: lesson 69 on trial designs and lesson 88 on reversible perturbation.
depth.mechanism:
The mechanism question can be decomposed into four scales, each with its own evidence.

At the scale of the membrane, the electric field changes the transmembrane potential of neurons near the contact. A brief pulse can open voltage-gated sodium channels and trigger an action potential in an axon, while the soma may be depolarised enough to enter a state of block. Because axons are more excitable than cell bodies to brief pulses, the direct effect is a mixture of activation of passing and projecting fibres and suppression of local somatic output. The mixture explains why the same electrode can reduce tremor and worsen dysarthria: different fibre populations are affected.

At the scale of the local circuit, high-frequency stimulation changes the firing pattern of the target nucleus. In the subthalamic nucleus, stimulation reduces the pathological bursting and oscillatory pattern that is correlated with rigidity and akinesia, and it increases the regularity of firing in downstream pallidal neurons. The change in pattern, rather than a change in mean rate, is a plausible candidate for the clinical effect, because lesions of the same nucleus produce similar but less adjustable benefit.

At the scale of the network, stimulation changes activity in cortex, thalamus and brainstem through orthodromic and antidromic effects. Imaging during stimulation shows changes in cortical motor areas and in the cerebellum, and stimulation can produce effects on non-motor functions, including mood and cognition, that are not explained by the target's classical motor role. That is why the target's anatomical label is a poor guide to its clinical effects.

At the scale of the biomarker, beta activity falls when stimulation is switched on, and the fall correlates with improvement across patients. Correlation across states is not causation, because stimulation changes many things at once, and the direction of the relationship is unresolved. The strongest current test is closed-loop stimulation, which delivers current only when beta exceeds a threshold: if suppressing beta is the mechanism, then a closed-loop protocol that keeps beta low with less current should produce comparable benefit with fewer side effects.
depth.secondExample:
Consider the dissociation between open-label and controlled results in psychiatric stimulation, because it is the cleanest case of a non-specific response masquerading as a treatment effect. In treatment-resistant depression, stimulation of the subcallosal cingulate region produced response rates of around 40 to 60 per cent in open-label series and was described as a breakthrough. A randomised, sham-controlled trial with a credible sham condition found no significant difference between active and sham arms at the primary endpoint.

There are three candidate explanations, and they make different predictions. The first is that the sham was not inert: if sham stimulation produced a real biological effect, the trial would underestimate the treatment. That explanation predicts a biological change in the sham arm, which can be tested with imaging or with a physiological marker. The second is that the open-label effect was non-specific: expectation, attention, the surgical procedure and the natural history of a fluctuating illness. That explanation predicts that response in the open-label series would be similar in patients whose devices were later found to be poorly positioned, which has been reported. The third is that the patient selection was different: the trial may have enrolled a more chronic, more treatment-resistant group, which predicts a lower response in both arms and does not explain the absence of a difference.

The instructive point is that the open-label series was not fraudulent and the trial was not necessarily wrong. They measured different quantities in different populations. The error was in the inference from the first to the second, and it is the same error that appears whenever a pre-post change is described as a treatment effect. The remedy is structural: pre-register the controlled comparison, report the success of blinding, and treat the open-label response as a hypothesis about who might benefit rather than as evidence that the intervention works.
depth.mistake:
The intuition that deep brain stimulation inhibits its target, the way a lesion would, is the source of most confusion here. The clinical benefit of high-frequency stimulation resembles the benefit of a lesion in some targets, which encouraged the inhibition story, but the physiology is mixed: somatic output may be suppressed while axons are activated, and downstream structures show increased and regularised firing rather than silence. The diagnostic question is whether the study measured the firing of the target's projection neurons during stimulation; if it measured only the clinical effect, the inhibition claim is an inference from similarity of outcome, which is weak.

A second over-reading is that the target's function is revealed by the effect of stimulating it. Stimulation acts on a volume of tissue, on fibres of passage and on networks, and the behavioural result reflects the whole system. Stimulating the subthalamic nucleus improves motor scores, but that does not mean the nucleus is the site of motor impairment; it means that the network containing the nucleus can be modulated to produce improvement.

A third over-reading treats the pre-post improvement as the treatment effect. This is the error that fills the clinical literature with effect sizes that do not replicate in controlled trials, and it is the one this lesson is designed to prevent.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. You are given a company press release stating that its closed-loop stimulation system produced a 60 per cent improvement in motor scores in an open-label study of 20 patients. Write four questions that would decide whether the claim is supported, then compare with the model.

Model questions. One, comparison: was there a control condition, and if not, what would the same patients have done without stimulation over the same period? Two, blinding: were the outcome assessors blind to stimulation status, and was the success of blinding measured? Three, mechanism: does the closed-loop algorithm actually reduce the biomarker it targets, and is the reduction correlated with the clinical change within participants rather than only across them? Four, generalisability: who were the 20 patients, how were they selected, and what happened to those who did not respond?

Then write the strongest defensible sentence. Something like: in an open-label series of 20 patients, a closed-loop system was associated with a 60 per cent improvement from baseline, which is consistent with a treatment effect but does not separate stimulation from surgery, attention and natural fluctuation; a randomised comparison with blinded assessment is required before the effect can be attributed to the algorithm. That sentence is less exciting than the press release and it is the one that would survive review.
depth.summary: Deep brain stimulation delivers brief, high-frequency pulses through an electrode whose field is local but whose effects are network-wide. The mechanism is plural: somatic suppression, axonal activation, disruption of pathological oscillations and neurochemical changes all contribute, in proportions that depend on the target and the condition. Clinical evidence must be read as a comparison, not as a change from baseline, because surgery, expectation and the microlesion effect are large. Open-label response rates of 40 to 60 per cent and controlled differences of 10 to 20 points can both be true, and the difference between them is the non-specific component that a trial is designed to remove.

lessons.title: Anaesthesia and the assessment of consciousness: responsiveness, experience, and what a complexity index can tell a family
lessons.explanation:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate wakefulness, awareness and responsiveness, describe how different anaesthetics produce unresponsiveness through different mechanisms, evaluate processed EEG indices and the perturbational complexity index, and explain why a group-validated classifier cannot answer a question about one patient. Lesson 71 established that a cellular mechanism can be argued to support consciousness without measuring it; lesson 60 established where the computer metaphor breaks. This lesson takes the clinical situation in which those questions become practical: a person who does not respond.

Three concepts must be separated before any measurement is discussed. Wakefulness is the state of being aroused, supported by the ascending arousal system and by the thalamus. Awareness is the having of experience, which is not directly observable. Responsiveness is the capacity to produce a behaviour on request, which is what a clinician assesses. These can dissociate in both directions. A person can be awake and aware but unable to move because of a neuromuscular blocker; a person can be unresponsive but aware, as in the isolated forearm technique; and a person can be responsive without awareness, as in automatisms and in some complex behaviours during sleep or seizure.

Anaesthesia produces unresponsiveness through several mechanisms, and they are not equivalent. Propofol potentiates GABA-A receptors, increasing the amplitude and duration of inhibitory currents, which suppresses cortical and thalamic activity and at higher doses produces burst suppression, a pattern in which periods of suppression alternate with bursts of activity. Volatile agents act on multiple channels, including GABA-A, glycine receptors and two-pore potassium channels, and they also depress thalamocortical transmission. Ketamine is an NMDA receptor antagonist that, at anaesthetic doses, produces a dissociative state with increased high-frequency cortical activity and vivid dreams, and it does not simply silence the cortex. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist that reduces locus coeruleus firing, which links this lesson to the noradrenergic system in lesson 82 and produces a state closer to natural sleep.

The neural correlates differ accordingly. Propofol anaesthesia is associated with a loss of long-range feedback connectivity from frontal to posterior regions while feedforward responses to a sensory stimulus may persist, with a shift of alpha power from posterior to anterior regions, and at deeper levels with burst suppression. Ketamine preserves or increases high-frequency activity and can preserve the complexity of the cortical response to a perturbation. The general lesson is that there is no single signature of unconsciousness, because the state can be produced by different pharmacological routes that converge on unresponsiveness without converging on the same electrophysiology.

Processed EEG indices such as the bispectral index are the most widely used clinical measures. They compress the EEG into a number from 0 to 100, derived from spectral and entropy features and calibrated against the concentration of anaesthetic and the probability of movement. They are useful for titrating drug delivery and for reducing the risk of overly deep anaesthesia. They are not measures of consciousness: they are affected by electromyographic activity, by age, by hypothermia, by other drugs and by artefacts, and they were validated against endpoints such as movement and recall rather than against experience.

The perturbational complexity index takes a different approach, and it is the most theoretically motivated measure in clinical use. A transcranial magnetic pulse perturbs the cortex, and high-density EEG records the response. The spatiotemporal pattern is compressed, and the compressibility is used as an index of how differentiated and integrated the response is. The logic is that a conscious brain produces a response that is both widespread and complex, while an unconscious brain produces a response that is either local or stereotyped. Casali and colleagues (Science Translational Medicine, 2013) introduced the index and tested it in wakefulness, dreaming, non-rapid eye movement sleep and sedation with several agents. Casarotto and colleagues (Annals of Neurology, 2016) validated it in 150 healthy controls and communicative brain-injured participants, then applied it to 38 patients in a minimally conscious state and 43 in a vegetative state, and reported that the index identified patients with preserved cortical complexity, including some who had been classified as vegetative.

The clinical interpretation is where the discipline is required. The index is a classifier trained on groups, with a threshold and an error rate, applied to an individual whose state can fluctuate. A value above the threshold is evidence of a capacity for complex cortical processing, not proof of experience; a value below it is evidence against that capacity at that moment, not proof of its absence. The measure also requires equipment, expertise and a patient who can tolerate a magnetic pulse. And the most important clinical evidence remains behavioural: repeated assessment, family observation, and purposeful responses that the bedside examination may miss.
lessons.example:
Work the arithmetic of a diagnostic test applied to a rare event, because that is the core of the awareness-monitoring problem.

Step 1, the test. Suppose a processed EEG index identifies awareness with 90 per cent sensitivity and 90 per cent specificity in a validation cohort where a substantial proportion of patients were aware. Those figures are optimistic but convenient.

Step 2, the prevalence. Explicit awareness under general anaesthesia is rare, on the order of one to two cases per thousand anaesthetics. Take 0.15 per cent as the prevalence in a general surgical population.

Step 3, the positive predictive value. With sensitivity 0.9, specificity 0.9 and prevalence 0.0015, the probability that a patient with a positive index is actually aware is 0.9 times 0.0015 divided by the sum of 0.9 times 0.0015 and 0.1 times 0.9985, which is about 0.013, or 1.3 per cent. In a thousand anaesthetics, the test generates about 100 false positives and one or two true positives.

Step 4, the negative predictive value. The same calculation gives a negative predictive value of about 0.9998, so a negative result is reassuring, which is why the test is more useful for ruling out than for ruling in.

Step 5, the dependence on prevalence. If the same test were used in a population with a 20 per cent prevalence, such as patients receiving a neuromuscular blocker with light sedation, the positive predictive value would rise to about 69 per cent. The test has not changed; the prior has. This is why a monitor validated in one context cannot be transplanted to another without re-evaluating its operating characteristics.

Step 6, the clinical implication. A monitor that reduces the depth of anaesthesia may reduce awareness by shifting the distribution of doses, even if its individual alerts are mostly false positives. That is a population-level benefit and a different claim from the ability to detect awareness in an individual. Both claims can be true, and a study that shows the first does not show the second.
lessons.question: A patient who has been unresponsive for three months after a traumatic brain injury has a complexity index above the threshold that separated conscious from unconscious volunteers in a validation study. The family asks whether this means the patient is conscious. Which answer is most defensible?
lessons.answer: It raises the probability that the patient has the cortical capacity for conscious processing at the time of testing, and it should prompt repeated assessment and a search for behavioural signs, but it is a probabilistic group-level result applied to one person and it does not establish that the patient is experiencing anything.
lessons.distractor: The index is above threshold, so the patient is conscious and should be treated as such in all decisions.
lessons.correction: The inference from a validated classifier to an individual's experience is the error. The threshold was chosen to separate groups, and at that threshold some controls fall below and some unconscious patients fall above. A single value also describes one moment, and disorders of consciousness fluctuate over hours and days. What the result does justify is a change in clinical posture: more frequent and more sensitive behavioural assessment, attention to signs such as visual tracking or command following that may be intermittent, and caution about prognoses based on a single examination. It does not justify the claim that the patient is conscious, and it does not remove the need for the family to be given the uncertainty honestly.

depth.definitions: Wakefulness is the state of arousal, supported by the ascending reticular activating system and thalamocortical circuits. Awareness is the having of subjective experience. Responsiveness is the capacity to produce a voluntary behaviour. Connected consciousness is experience of the environment, as distinct from disconnected consciousness such as dreaming. The isolated forearm technique inflates a tourniquet before neuromuscular blockade so that a patient can move a hand to signal awareness. The bispectral index is a processed EEG value from 0 to 100 derived from spectral and entropy features. Burst suppression is an EEG pattern of alternating high-amplitude bursts and flat periods, seen at deep anaesthesia. The perturbational complexity index is derived from the spatiotemporal complexity of the cortical response to a transcranial magnetic pulse, measured with high-density EEG. Sensitivity is the proportion of aware patients correctly identified, specificity the proportion of unaware patients correctly identified, and positive predictive value the proportion of positive tests that are true positives. Prerequisites: lesson 71 on argued mechanisms and lesson 60 on the computer metaphor.
depth.mechanism:
The mechanisms by which anaesthetics abolish responsiveness converge on thalamocortical and corticocortical communication, but they start at different receptors.

GABAergic agents such as propofol increase the duration and amplitude of inhibitory postsynaptic currents, which reduces the probability that a thalamic or cortical neuron reaches threshold in response to input. At low doses this reduces the gain of thalamocortical transfer; at higher doses it produces a state in which cortical neurons are synchronised in slow oscillations and then in burst suppression. The result is a brain that still responds to a stimulus at the periphery but does not propagate the response across cortex.

NMDA antagonists such as ketamine reduce excitatory transmission onto inhibitory interneurons, which paradoxically increases activity in some cortical circuits, and they disrupt the coincidence detection that supports recurrent processing. The result is a state in which the cortex is active and the EEG shows high-frequency power, but the pattern of activity is not integrated in the way that supports connected experience of the environment.

Alpha-2 agonists such as dexmedetomidine reduce noradrenergic drive from the locus coeruleus, which reduces arousal without the GABAergic synchrony of propofol. Volatile agents act at several sites, including two-pore potassium channels that hyperpolarise neurons and glycine receptors in the spinal cord, which is why they produce immobility at concentrations lower than those required for amnesia.

The convergence is at the level of network integration. A conscious state requires that information be represented in a way that is both differentiated, so that many states are possible, and integrated, so that the representation is available to many processes. Anaesthetics reduce one or both: GABAergic agents reduce differentiation by producing synchrony and then silence, while ketamine may preserve differentiation but disrupt the recurrent integration that makes information globally available. That is the framework in which a complexity measure makes sense, and it is also why the same number can mean different things under different drugs.
depth.secondExample:
The comparison between propofol and ketamine is the clearest natural experiment in this field, and it is worth working through because it shows how a dissociation constrains theory.

Under propofol, volunteers become unresponsive, the complexity index falls below the threshold observed in wakefulness, and the EEG shows slow and alpha activity with loss of long-range feedback. Under ketamine, volunteers also become unresponsive, but the complexity index can remain within the waking range, high-frequency activity increases, and many volunteers report vivid dreams or out-of-body experiences afterwards. Two states with the same behavioural endpoint have opposite signatures on the measure.

There are three ways to read this. The first is that the index measures something real about cortical integration, and the ketamine state is one in which integration persists while the capacity to respond is abolished; the reports of experience support that reading. The second is that the index is sensitive to the drug rather than to consciousness, so it cannot be used across agents without recalibration. The third is that responsiveness and experience are simply different constructs, and the ketamine case is evidence for that rather than a problem for the measure. The three readings are not mutually exclusive, and the experiment cannot choose between them without an independent report of experience, which is exactly what the volunteers provide.

The practical consequence is that any clinical use of a complexity measure must specify the anaesthetic. A threshold derived from propofol sedation may not apply during ketamine sedation or during recovery from a volatile agent. That is not a defect of the measure; it is a property of a biological index that depends on the mechanism producing the state.
depth.mistake:
The most common over-reading is that a processed EEG number measures consciousness. The bispectral index was developed to predict the probability of movement and of recall under specific anaesthetics, and it is affected by muscle activity, by age, by temperature and by other drugs. A value in the recommended range is evidence about the dose of anaesthetic, not about whether the patient is experiencing anything. The diagnostic question is what the index was calibrated against; if the answer is movement or drug concentration, the index cannot be a consciousness meter.

A second over-reading equates unresponsiveness with unconsciousness. The isolated forearm experiments show that a substantial minority of patients can signal awareness during light anaesthesia, and the disorders of consciousness literature contains patients who recover despite a vegetative state diagnosis. Behaviour is a narrow channel, and its absence is weak evidence about experience.

A third over-reading treats a single brain region or a single rhythm as the seat of consciousness. The theoretical proposals differ: global workspace theory emphasises a network ignition that broadcasts information, integrated information theory emphasises the causal structure of a system, and recurrent processing theory emphasises feedback within sensory cortex. Each makes different predictions about which measure should track experience, and none has been decisively confirmed. A claim that one area or one frequency is the correlate of consciousness should be read as a proposal within a theory.
depth.application:
Nonblocking task. A hospital proposes to buy a depth-of-anaesthesia monitor to prevent intraoperative awareness. Write a four-part appraisal, then compare with the model.

Model appraisal. One, the outcome: what does the device measure, and against what endpoint was it validated? If the validation endpoint was movement or drug concentration, the device cannot be marketed as an awareness detector without a trial using explicit recall as the outcome.

Two, the operating characteristics: what are the sensitivity and specificity at the recommended threshold, and what is the prevalence of awareness in this hospital's case mix? Compute the positive predictive value, and state how many false alerts a thousand anaesthetics would generate.

Three, the evidence of benefit: has a randomised trial shown that using the monitor reduces awareness compared with a protocol based on end-tidal agent concentration? If the trial exists, what was the absolute risk reduction and the number needed to treat?

Four, the implementation: who will interpret the alerts, what will they do differently, and what are the costs of false alerts, including deeper anaesthesia and its own risks? Then write the recommendation in one sentence, separating the population-level benefit from the individual-level diagnostic claim.
depth.summary: Wakefulness, awareness and responsiveness are distinct, and anaesthesia dissociates them: propofol silences cortex through GABAergic inhibition, ketamine produces unresponsiveness with a wake-like cortex, and dexmedetomidine reduces noradrenergic arousal. Processed EEG indices are dose monitors, not consciousness meters, and complexity indices measure the integration and differentiation of a perturbation with a group-derived threshold. Applied to an individual, any such index shifts a probability and should change clinical behaviour, not settle a metaphysical question. The honest clinical answer combines the number, the drug, the time course and repeated behaviour.

Print the arithmetic for a prevalence of 20 per cent, which gives about 69 per cent, and label the difference THE PRIOR MATTERS.

Step 6 SINGLE PATIENT (right bottom): a flow from TEST RESULT above threshold to REPEAT ASSESSMENT, FAMILY OBSERVATION, SEARCH FOR TRACKING AND COMMAND FOLLOWING, and PROBABILISTIC DISCUSSION. Add the warning box ONE VALUE, ONE MOMENT, ONE GROUP-DERIVED THRESHOLD.

Step 7 SUMMARY STRIP (bottom): three statements, PROPOFOL AND KETAMINE REACH THE SAME BEHAVIOURAL ENDPOINT BY DIFFERENT ROUTES, NO SINGLE EEG SIGNATURE DEFINES UNCONSCIOUSNESS, and A MONITOR CHANGES A PROBABILITY AND DOES NOT SETTLE EXPERIENCE.

questions.prompt: An intracranial study reports that hippocampal theta power predicts successful recall. The cohort is 12 patients, but 760 of the 900 analysed electrodes come from two patients with extensive hippocampal coverage, and the effect is significant when electrodes are treated as independent observations. What is the main threat to the claim?
questions.answer: Pseudoreplication: electrodes are nested within patients, so the effective sample size is closer to 12 than to 900, and the result may reflect the anatomy and seizure history of two individuals rather than a general property of the human hippocampus.
questions.distractor: The electrode count is large enough that sampling error is negligible; the only remaining concern is whether theta was measured with the right filter settings.
questions.correction: The over-reading is to count electrodes as participants. Electrodes within one patient share the same brain, the same electrode type, the same reference and often the same pathology, so they are not independent draws from a population. With 760 of 900 electrodes in two patients, a patient-level analysis could show an effect in two of twelve people. The repair is a mixed model with patient as a random effect, a leave-one-patient-out analysis, and explicit reporting of how many patients contribute to each effect; the number of electrodes is a statement about spatial sampling, not about generalisability.

questions.prompt: A study of 17 participants images brain activity while they watch animated shapes, reports a cluster of 412 voxels in the temporoparietal junction at a corrected threshold, and the press release states that the region is where the brain represents the intentions of others. Which criticism is most warranted?
questions.answer: The cluster establishes that a spatially extended set of voxels responded more in one condition, but it does not establish a selective function for the region, and cluster extent inference with a liberal forming threshold can be invalid when the spatial autocorrelation does not match the assumed shape.
questions.distractor: The finding is sound because the cluster survived correction for multiple comparisons, so the only issue is whether the task really engaged mentalising.
questions.correction: Corrected significance answers a question about noise, not about function. A cluster of 412 voxels at 3 mm resolution spans well over a cubic centimetre and contains hundreds of thousands of neurons plus white matter, vessels and multiple cytoarchitectonic areas, so the spatial label is a coarse anatomical guess. The functional label requires selectivity: the same region should respond to a comparison task that does not require mentalising, and the reverse inference has to be probabilistic rather than definitional. Cluster inference adds a second problem, because its validity depends on the spatial autocorrelation matching the parametric assumption, which is exactly the assumption that fails in the analyses reported by Eklund and colleagues.

questions.prompt: Single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex at 300 ms after stimulus onset slows responses on a working memory task, while stimulation over the vertex and sham stimulation have no effect. The authors conclude that the region stores the memory trace. Which alternative interpretation is strongest?
questions.answer: The result shows that activity in the stimulated region is necessary at that moment for efficient performance, which is compatible with a role in manipulating or selecting information rather than in storing it; storage would need evidence that the information is present in the region's activity pattern.
questions.distractor: Because stimulation disrupted performance and a control site did not, the region must hold the memory representation for the duration of the delay.
questions.correction: Necessity at a time point is being converted into a storage function. A virtual lesion demonstrates that the tissue under the coil contributes to performance in the tested window; it does not show what the tissue represents, and it cannot distinguish storage from retrieval, attention, or response selection. The coil also stimulates a volume of cortex roughly a centimetre across, activates fibres of passage and can spread transsynaptically, so the effective lesion is not confined to the named region. Storage claims need a decoding test or a recording that shows the information in that tissue, ideally combined with the disruption.

questions.prompt: An open-label series of subthalamic deep brain stimulation in Parkinson disease reports a 45 per cent improvement in motor scores at six months. A later randomised trial with sham stimulation reports a 22 per cent improvement on active stimulation and a 12 per cent improvement on sham. What best explains the discrepancy?
questions.answer: Open-label improvement combines stimulation effects with expectation, attention and the microlesion effect of electrode insertion, all of which the sham-controlled design partly removes, so the unbiased estimate of the stimulation-specific effect is the difference between arms rather than the change from baseline.
questions.distractor: The randomised trial under-dosed patients, because open-label studies use higher amplitudes and longer follow-up, so the 45 per cent figure is closer to the true effect.
questions.correction: The over-reading is to treat the pre-post change in an unblinded series as the treatment effect. Patients who have undergone surgery expect to improve, clinicians who programmed the device rate differently, and insertion alone produces a measurable improvement before any current is delivered. The randomised comparison estimates the incremental effect of stimulation over the procedure, which is a different and smaller quantity. Neither number is wrong; they answer different questions. The report should state which quantity is being claimed, because a 45 per cent pre-post improvement and a 10-point between-arm difference can both be true of the same cohort.

questions.prompt: A patient with a severe brain injury is unresponsive to commands. A processed EEG index reads 45, within the range the manufacturer labels as adequate anaesthesia. A perturbational complexity index obtained with transcranial magnetic stimulation and high-density EEG is below the threshold that separated conscious from unconscious volunteers in the validation study. The family asks whether the patient is conscious. What is the best answer?
questions.answer: The complexity index provides probabilistic evidence about the capacity for conscious processing rather than a direct readout of experience, and it should be interpreted alongside repeated behavioural assessment, because unresponsiveness, disconnected consciousness and unconsciousness are different states that can dissociate.
questions.distractor: The processed EEG index shows an anaesthetic-level value, so the patient is unconscious and the complexity result can be set aside as technical noise.
questions.correction: Two category errors are available here, and the distractor commits the more common one. A depth-of-anaesthesia index is a processed spectral ratio validated against drug concentration and movement, not a measure of experience, and it is vulnerable to electromyographic artifact, temperature and sedative drugs. The complexity index is better grounded, because it perturbs cortex and measures the spatiotemporal complexity of the response, but it is a group-validated classifier applied to an individual, with a cutoff and an error rate. The defensible statement is probabilistic, it distinguishes capacity from content, and it does not overrule bedside evidence of connected consciousness such as purposefully tracking the clinician's face.

questions.prompt: Hippocampal theta in a rat runs at 7 Hz while gamma runs at 60 Hz. During a spatial choice, gamma amplitude is greatest at the trough of theta. If the coupling is real, how many gamma cycles fit within one theta cycle, and what would a report that one gamma burst occurs per theta cycle imply about the coupling?
questions.answer: About 8.6 gamma cycles fit in one 143 ms theta cycle, so a single gamma burst per theta cycle is a sparse, phase-specific relationship rather than continuous amplitude modulation, and the ratio should be reported with the phase of peak amplitude.
questions.distractor: About 2 gamma cycles fit in one theta cycle, so the coupling indicates that each theta cycle contains two independent gamma events.
questions.correction: The arithmetic error is a common one: 60 divided by 7 is 8.6, not 2, and the 143 ms period follows from 1000 divided by 7. The conceptual error is to conflate the number of cycles with the number of bursts. A coupling index computed on a 60 Hz band describes how amplitude varies with theta phase; the number of bursts per cycle describes a different quantity, namely how often the modulation peaks. Both must be stated, and neither establishes that the gamma activity is transferred to another region. The cycle ratio is a constraint on mechanism, because a gamma burst that lasts one cycle cannot carry information across a whole theta phase.

questions.prompt: Participants perform a contrast discrimination task. Those with high pre-stimulus tonic pupil diameter show worse discrimination and larger response variability, while those with intermediate diameter perform best, and a phasic pupil response to the stimulus predicts faster correct responses. Which framework organises these results?
questions.answer: An inverted-U relation in which tonic arousal sets the gain of cortical responding: intermediate tonic activity supports discrimination, high tonic activity increases variability and favours disengagement, and the phasic response reflects a transient gain increase to the stimulus.
questions.distractor: Pupil diameter indexes effort, so the high-tonic group performed worse because they were trying harder and became distracted.
questions.correction: The effort account is an unmeasured mentalistic explanation that has no independent variable; it also predicts that more effort should improve performance, which contradicts the observed pattern. The inverted-U account makes the opposite prediction and specifies a mechanism, namely gain modulation of sensory responses by noradrenergic input, with behavioural consequences for the signal-to-noise ratio of the discrimination. The remaining caveat is that pupil diameter is not a pure index of locus coeruleus activity: it is controlled by both sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways, it responds to light, and it is affected by arousal from many sources. The result is consistent with the framework and does not measure the nucleus.

questions.prompt: Rats receive selective immunotoxic lesions of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons and are tested on a five-choice serial reaction time task. They make more omission errors and have slower correct responses, but accuracy on trials they complete is unchanged, and performance falls further when the inter-trial interval is made variable. What is the best interpretation?
questions.answer: The pattern points to a deficit in attentional capture and response readiness rather than in discrimination, because accuracy conditional on responding is spared while omissions and timing-dependent performance deteriorate.
questions.distractor: The lesion impaired memory, since the animals failed to complete trials and therefore could not remember the correct response.
questions.correction: Omissions are being read as memory failure when they are equally consistent with a failure to sustain or deploy attention. The dissociation inside the data is the informative part: if the animals could not discriminate, accuracy on completed trials should fall; it did not. The sensitivity to variable inter-trial intervals adds a timing and arousal component. Two further limits apply. Immunotoxic lesions remove cholinergic neurons but also produce inflammation and can damage non-cholinergic elements, so the lesion is not molecularly specific. And the basal forebrain contains GABAergic and glutamatergic projection neurons that also contribute to cortical state, so attributing the whole behavioural profile to acetylcholine requires cell-type-specific manipulation.

questions.prompt: A drug that is a substrate of P-glycoprotein at the blood-brain barrier is given with a second drug that inhibits P-glycoprotein. Brain concentrations of the first drug rise tenfold while plasma concentrations rise only 1.3-fold. A commentary describes this as proof that the barrier is failing in patients with inflammation. What is wrong with the commentary?
questions.answer: The experiment shows that an efflux transporter was limiting brain entry, which is a normal regulated function of the barrier; calling it barrier failure confuses transporter inhibition with loss of tight-junction integrity.
questions.distractor: The tenfold rise in brain concentration shows that the barrier had already broken down, since a healthy barrier would exclude the drug entirely.
questions.correction: A healthy barrier is not an impermeable wall. It is a set of endothelial tight junctions plus a large family of transporters that actively extrude lipophilic molecules, and P-glycoprotein is one of them. Inhibiting the transporter increases brain penetration without any change in tight-junction integrity, so the finding is evidence for transporter-mediated restriction, not for leakage. The separate plasma change of 1.3-fold is important, because it shows that most of the brain effect cannot be explained by systemic exposure. A leakage claim would require a marker of junctional integrity, such as a quantitative albumin ratio, and a region where the barrier is normally tight.

questions.prompt: Patients receiving interferon-alpha for hepatitis C develop depression at a higher rate than controls, and pretreatment with an antidepressant reduces the incidence. A review concludes that inflammation causes depression. Which refinement is required?
questions.answer: The trial supports a causal contribution of cytokine signalling to a depressive syndrome in a clinical population, but the effect is conditional on dose, vulnerability and treatment context, and it does not establish that inflammation is the cause of depression in general.
questions.distractor: Since blocking the effect pharmacologically prevented depression, inflammation is established as the cause of major depression.
questions.correction: Prevention by an antidepressant is evidence that the syndrome is modifiable, not that inflammation is the cause of the syndrome in every population. Interferon-alpha produces a specific cytokine-driven state with fatigue, anhedonia and cognitive slowing, which overlaps with depression but is not identical to it, and the preventive drug has its own mechanisms. The inference also ignores individual differences: most treated patients do not become depressed, so the causal statement needs a moderator, such as baseline inflammatory markers or prior vulnerability. The defensible claim is that cytokine signalling can produce a depressive phenotype in some people, and that this is a model for a subtype, not a general aetiology.

questions.prompt: A human single-unit study records from the medial temporal lobe in 9 patients with epilepsy and reports neurons that respond selectively to images of the actress Jennifer Aniston. What can be concluded about the representation of familiar people in the human brain?
questions.answer: The recordings establish that some human medial temporal neurons respond selectively to particular familiar individuals, which constrains theories of representation, but the sample is small, drawn from a clinical population, and cannot establish the format or the prevalence of such coding.
questions.distractor: The existence of a Jennifer Aniston neuron shows that the brain stores each familiar person in a single dedicated cell.
questions.correction: The over-reading is the leap from a selective response to a dedicated storage unit. A cell that responds to one person also typically responds to related images, and its response depends on the task and on the patient's experience; selectivity in a sampled population is not exclusivity, and the recorded neurons are a tiny, clinically selected fraction of the region. The result is nonetheless valuable because it is a direct measurement in humans of sparse, invariant responses, which animal work could not provide for a personally familiar face. What it cannot do is estimate how many such cells exist, whether they are necessary for recognition, or whether the same organisation holds outside epilepsy.

questions.prompt: A single patient with a rare lesion is scanned while viewing faces. The contrast of faces versus houses produces a strong left fusiform cluster. The authors publish it as a case study locating the face area. Colleagues note that repeating the scan in the same patient on a second day produces a cluster in a different location. What does this imply?
questions.answer: The between-session instability shows that a single-subject map is not a reliable localiser, so the case can motivate a hypothesis but cannot establish the location of a function without a replication sample and a reliability estimate.
questions.distractor: The second scan failed because the patient was tired, so the first result stands as the valid localisation.
questions.correction: Choosing the session that produced the cleaner map is an example of analysis flexibility, and it converts noise into a finding. Single-subject fMRI has low reliability for fine spatial patterns, particularly with small numbers of events, and a lesion changes vasculature and registration, which adds further variance. A localiser claim needs a within-subject reliability estimate across sessions, a group replication, and a stated spatial precision. The case study remains useful for the questions it raises about the patient's perception, but it cannot carry a localisation claim on its own.

questions.prompt: One hertz repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation over the left parietal cortex for 20 minutes reduces performance on a number comparison task for 15 minutes afterwards, while stimulation over the right parietal cortex and sham stimulation have no effect. A reviewer asks how many pulses were delivered and what the after-effect demonstrates.
questions.answer: The protocol delivered 1200 pulses (1 Hz for 1200 seconds), and the after-effect demonstrates that disrupting the left parietal region transiently impairs task performance, which is a necessity claim about a time-averaged contribution rather than about the specific computation.
questions.distractor: The protocol delivered 20 pulses, one per minute, and the after-effect demonstrates that the left parietal cortex stores numerical magnitude.
questions.correction: The pulse arithmetic is the easy error: 1 Hz means one pulse per second, so 20 minutes is 1200 seconds and therefore 1200 pulses. The conceptual error is to convert a disruption into a storage claim. Low-frequency stimulation reduces excitability in the stimulated region and in connected regions for minutes after the train, so the effect is a temporary lesion with an unknown spatial and network footprint. It shows that the region was needed, on average, during the task; it does not show which operation was performed, and it does not exclude a role for connected areas that the stimulation also influenced.

questions.prompt: Intraoperative recordings from the subthalamic nucleus in Parkinson patients show that local field potential power in the beta band (13 to 30 Hz) falls when dopaminergic medication is given and when therapeutic stimulation is switched on, and that beta power correlates with rigidity scores. A paper concludes that beta oscillations cause parkinsonian rigidity. Which issue is most important?
questions.answer: The correlation across states is consistent with beta activity as a marker or contributor, but causation requires manipulation of beta independently of medication and stimulation and a demonstration that rigidity follows the manipulation, because both interventions change many things at once.
questions.distractor: The fact that two independent interventions both reduce beta power and rigidity shows that beta is the common causal pathway.
questions.correction: Two interventions converging on the same correlate is suggestive, not conclusive, because each intervention has many effects and the correlation could be a downstream consequence of rigidity rather than its cause. The logic also fails to exclude a third variable, such as altered thalamocortical drive, that changes both beta and tone. What the data establish is that beta power tracks the parkinsonian state and that it is a useful feedback signal for adaptive stimulation. Causal language would need a manipulation that targets beta selectively, for instance phase-specific closed-loop stimulation, with a pre-specified test of whether the behavioural change follows the oscillatory change in time.

questions.prompt: Under propofol sedation, a volunteer is unresponsive and has low perturbational complexity. Under ketamine, a volunteer is also unresponsive but has complexity values within the range seen in wakefulness, and reports vivid dreams afterwards. What does this dissociation imply for the use of complexity as a consciousness measure?
questions.answer: It implies that complexity tracks the integrated capacity for conscious processing rather than behavioural responsiveness, and that unresponsiveness can coexist with a wake-like complexity and with reported experience, so the index must be interpreted with the drug and the state in mind.
questions.distractor: It implies that ketamine does not actually produce unconsciousness, so the ketamine condition should be excluded from validation studies.
questions.correction: Excluding the discordant condition would remove the most informative case. The dissociation is the evidence that responsiveness and experience come apart: ketamine produces a state in which the subject does not respond but later reports experience, and the high complexity value is consistent with that report. Propofol, by contrast, reduces complexity along with responsiveness. The correct conclusion is that a complexity index is a state classifier whose meaning depends on the anaesthetic mechanism, not a universal meter of experience, and that any clinical use must specify the drug, the dose and the behavioural assessment alongside the number.

questions.prompt: You want to test whether theta-gamma coupling in the human hippocampus is necessary for memory encoding. You have access to intracranial electrodes in epilepsy patients and to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation. Which design best supports a causal claim?
questions.answer: Measure coupling during encoding with intracranial electrodes, then use stimulation time-locked to the theta phase to disrupt the gamma burst in a subset of trials, and test whether the disruption reduces coupling and subsequently reduces recall of those specific items.
questions.distractor: Stimulate the hippocampus at gamma frequency and show that recall improves, since improving memory demonstrates that the coupled rhythm is the mechanism.
questions.correction: Improving performance with stimulation shows that the tissue can be driven to produce a behavioural benefit, not that the endogenous coupling mediates encoding. The causal design needs three features: a within-trial manipulation that targets the coupling rather than the region as a whole, a measured effect of the manipulation on the coupling index, and an item-specific behavioural consequence that follows in time. Phase-locked stimulation approximates this, but it also requires a control that delivers the same total current at random phases, because current delivery alone changes local excitability. The intracranial measurement then serves as the mediator, which is what turns a stimulation effect into a mechanistic claim.

questions.prompt: A team proposes to test whether locus coeruleus noradrenergic activity sharpens cortical orientation tuning in humans. They plan to use pupil diameter as the index of locus coeruleus activity, a 7-tesla scan to localise the nucleus, and a placebo-controlled beta blocker to manipulate noradrenergic signalling. Which limitation most needs to be addressed in the design?
questions.answer: All three measures are indirect and none is specific to the locus coeruleus: pupil diameter integrates multiple arousal pathways, the brainstem signal is contaminated by nearby vasculature and motion, and a systemic beta blocker acts at many receptors throughout the body and brain, so the design needs converging measures and a manipulation that can dissociate noradrenergic from general arousal.
questions.distractor: The design is sound because the three measures triangulate the same construct, and agreement among them would establish that noradrenaline sharpens tuning.
questions.correction: Agreement among indirect measures can reflect a shared confound rather than a shared mechanism, since all three are sensitive to arousal, effort and autonomic state. The 7-tesla localiser improves anatomical precision but does not make a small brainstem nucleus immune to vascular and motion artefact, and pupil diameter is driven by both sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow. A beta blocker is systemic and central effects are mixed with peripheral ones, including cardiovascular changes that alter the pupil. The design would be strengthened by a task that separates gain from arousal, by a noradrenergic measure that is not pupil, and by a manipulation with a known site of action, with the primary hypothesis specified in advance.
